entities.title: Alcibiades
entities.description:
Alcibiades was an Athenian politician and commander whose career crossed the divisions of the Peloponnesian War. Brought up under Pericles’ guardianship, he became closely associated with Socrates.

He helped persuade Athens to send its great expedition to Sicily, then fled to Sparta after being recalled for trial. His later return to Athenian service makes his life a useful way through the war’s changing alliances.
entities.note: Approximate lifespan: sources give 451/450–404/403 BCE. The timeline uses 450–404, so age comparisons are approximate.

entities.title: Pericles
entities.description:
Pericles was an Athenian politician and commander, born around 495 BCE. His career belonged to the period when Athens became a dominant power in the Greek world.

He was still leading the city at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the epidemic in 429 BCE, early in a conflict that would continue for another quarter of a century.
entities.note: Approximate birth year; lifespan, not a reign. Athens was a democracy, and Pericles was not its monarch.

entities.title: Nicias
entities.description:
Nicias was an Athenian commander and politician who favoured peace with Sparta. The treaty negotiated in 421 BCE bears his name.

He opposed the proposed expedition to Sicily but nevertheless became one of its commanders alongside Alcibiades and Lamachus. His career ended with the expedition’s defeat in 413 BCE.
entities.note: Born around 470 BCE; died in 413 BCE. The opening decades of his life are poorly documented.

entities.title: Sparta
entities.description:
Sparta led the coalition fighting Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Its victory in 404 BCE forced Athens to give up its empire.

Alcibiades’ connection takes you inside that rivalry: after leaving Athenian service, he sought refuge with the Spartans and advised them against his own city.
entities.note: 450–404 BCE is this entry’s study window, not the founding or end of Sparta. The point locates the city, not Spartan territory. Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory.

entities.title: Syracuse
entities.description:
Syracuse was the principal target of the Athenian expedition to Sicily. Its defenders, aided by the Spartan commander Gylippus, resisted the siege.

The Athenian expedition was destroyed in 413 BCE. Syracuse’s connections show this part of the war from the city being attacked, rather than only from Athens.
entities.note: 415–413 BCE is an editorial campaign window, not the lifespan of the city. The marker uses Ortygia’s UNESCO reference point. UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position.

entities.title: The Peloponnesian War
entities.description:
The Peloponnesian War set Athens and its allies against Sparta and its coalition. It ran from 431 to 404 BCE, with a negotiated peace interrupting the main conflict.

Fighting extended well beyond the two cities. The Sicilian expedition and Persian involvement are part of the same history. Athens eventually surrendered and lost its empire.
entities.note: Overall war chronology. This span does not mean uninterrupted fighting in every region.

entities.title: The epidemic at Athens
entities.description:
A severe epidemic struck Athens during the early years of the war. People had crowded into the city for protection, and the disease killed soldiers and civilians, including Pericles in 429 BCE.

Thucydides survived it and described what he saw. The illness is conventionally called the plague of Athens, but its precise cause remains uncertain.
entities.note: Outbreaks between 430 and 426 BCE, not a claim of constant intensity. No modern diagnosis is presented as settled. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Socrates and Alcibiades at Potidaea
entities.description:
Socrates and Alcibiades were deployed to Potidaea in 432 BCE. Socrates served as a hoplite, an infantry soldier.

The episode places their relationship in military service as well as philosophical conversation.
entities.note: Deployment year. The campaign and siege continued afterwards; this entry does not date every episode associated with them.

entities.title: The battle of Delium
entities.description:
Socrates fought at Delium in 424 BCE, when the Athenian army was defeated.

Plato’s dialogues later present Alcibiades and Laches praising his conduct during the retreat. These are literary accounts of the event, not transcripts made on the battlefield.
entities.note: Battle year; testimony about Socrates is identified as coming through Plato.

entities.title: The Peace of Nicias
entities.description:
Athens and Sparta agreed to peace in 421 BCE after ten years of war. Nicias was closely associated with the negotiations.

The settlement did not resolve the rivalries between the cities and their allies. The later Sicilian expedition and renewed war show how limited the peace proved.
entities.note: Treaty concluded in March 421 BCE; not the final end of the Peloponnesian War.

entities.title: The Sicilian expedition
entities.description:
Athens sent a major expedition to Sicily in 415 BCE. Alcibiades, Nicias and Lamachus shared the initial command.

Alcibiades was recalled, and the remaining commanders pursued the campaign against Syracuse. Despite reinforcements, the expedition ended in disaster in 413 BCE. Many survivors became prisoners.
entities.note: Campaign dates. The Syracuse marker represents a principal target, not every landing or battle in Sicily. UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position.

entities.title: The mutilation of the herms
entities.description:
Just before the fleet sailed for Sicily, sacred stone figures called herms were mutilated across Athens. The attack provoked an investigation into sacrilege.

Alcibiades became caught up in accusations concerning religious offences. Accusations against him should not be read as proof that he personally damaged the herms.
entities.note: 415 BCE. The herm mutilations and accusations concerning the Mysteries were connected investigations, not identical charges. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Alcibiades turns to Sparta
entities.description:
Recalled from Sicily for trial in 415 BCE, Alcibiades escaped to Sparta. He advised Athens’ enemies as the war widened.

By 412 BCE he was helping Spartan operations in Ionia. This was a changing political allegiance, not an uninterrupted stay in the city of Sparta.
entities.note: Broad phase of Spartan cooperation, 415–412 BCE. The city marker indicates his refuge, not his location in every year. Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory.

entities.title: The coup of the Four Hundred
entities.description:
An oligarchic coup replaced Athenian democracy with the government of the Four Hundred in 411 BCE. Hopes of obtaining Persian support formed part of the political manoeuvring.

Alcibiades was involved in proposals linking a change of government to his own return. The new regime was divided from the start.
entities.note: Coup year. The Four Hundred were a different regime from the Thirty of 404 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Alcibiades returns to Athens
entities.description:
Alcibiades returned to Athens in 407 BCE after years away from the city.

His return belongs to the war’s final phase. It did not end the conflict, which continued until Athens’ defeat in 404 BCE.
entities.note: Return to the city, distinct from his earlier return to command of Athenian forces. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The generals’ trial after Arginusae
entities.description:
After the naval victory at Arginusae in 406 BCE, Athens prosecuted the commanders over the failure to recover men and bodies from the sea.

Socrates opposed the unlawful collective proceedings. Six generals were executed.
entities.note: Trial in Athens, not a marker for the battle at sea. This is distinct from Socrates’ own trial in 399 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The battle of Aegospotami
entities.description:
Lysander defeated the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE.

The defeat was followed by the siege of Athens. The city surrendered the following year.
entities.note: Naval defeat in 405 BCE. No precise battlefield coordinates are asserted.

entities.title: Athens surrenders to Sparta
entities.description:
Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, ending the Peloponnesian War. Its Long Walls were demolished.

Peace did not immediately restore political stability. The government of the Thirty and a civil conflict followed.
entities.note: Surrender in spring 404 BCE, displayed at year resolution. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The Thirty rule Athens
entities.description:
After Athens’ defeat, an oligarchic government known as the Thirty took power with Spartan backing. Opposition to its rule developed into civil war.

The regime was short-lived. Democratic forces recovered ground, and a settlement in 403 BCE restored democracy.
entities.note: Government of 404–403 BCE, not a lifespan. Its aftermath provides context for Socrates’ later trial without claiming a single cause for his prosecution. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Democracy returns to Athens
entities.description:
A settlement in 403 BCE restored Athenian democracy after the rule of the Thirty and the fighting that followed. The Spartan king Pausanias intervened in the reconciliation.

Socrates’ trial belongs to this restored democracy, four years later. The two events should not be collapsed into one.
entities.note: Restoration in 403 BCE. Socrates’ separate trial entry is dated 399 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The reign of Darius II
entities.description:
Darius II ruled the Persian Empire during the later years of the Peloponnesian War. His officials negotiated with Sparta, and Persian money helped support its fleet.

This places the war within a wider struggle over influence in the Aegean and western Anatolia. Persia was an active participant, not just a distant background.
entities.note: Reign, not lifespan. The displayed 423–404 BCE follows Livius; the accession falls across 424/423 BCE.

entities.title: Amyrtaeus challenges Persian rule in Egypt
entities.description:
Around 404 BCE, Amyrtaeus established himself as an Egyptian ruler and began consolidating independence from Persia. He was the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty.

The change did not happen everywhere at once. Documents from Elephantine still recognised the Persian king as late as 401 BCE. This is a gradual political transition, despite the single date on the timeline.
entities.note: Approximate accession date, not the instant liberation of all Egypt. The end of his reign is outside this entry’s scope.
